passage: Anirban, sit, you look like the sky fell on you. You forgot the load-test steps in front of the client, yes? Listen to your old Rashmi didi. When I was twenty-four, at the textile testing lab in Surat, I forgot how to calibrate the colour machine. I had done it every day in training, then not once for two months. My hands just stopped. I wanted the floor to swallow me. But I had a small green notebook in my apron. Every Monday I read one page of it, and once a month I redid the rare jobs from it. So I opened the notebook, followed my own steps, and finished. The lab head only said, "Good, you wrote it down." That night I stopped calling myself careless. The mind drops what it does not use. You just leave a trail back.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi work when she forgot how to calibrate the colour machine?
qa.a: She worked at the textile testing lab in Surat.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when her hands stopped at the colour machine?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and panicked, wanting the floor to swallow her, because she had done the job every day in training and expected it to stay.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned the moment around?
qa.a: Rashmi opened her green notebook and followed her own written steps instead of guessing, which worked because she had kept reviewing it on Mondays.

qa.q: How might the lab head have seen Rashmi's slip?
qa.a: The lab head seems to see it as ordinary, not as failure; writing it down mattered more than remembering it perfectly.

grounding: Shows a young worker using notes and regular review to recover a rarely used skill and treating the lapse as normal rather than as failure.

passage: The power went out at the recording studio at 4:50, ten minutes before the choir from Reena's school was due. The generator kicked in, but the big mixing desk reset to factory settings. Payal stared at it. She had last patched a twelve-voice choir in March, and now the order of the cables was simply gone. Her phone was at two percent, so the notes app was no help. For a second her chest tightened. Then she remembered the laminated card taped inside the second drawer, the one she rewrote every few weeks. She pulled it out, traced each line with her finger, and began plugging in. "Of course I forgot," she muttered. "I haven't touched this since March." When Reena walked in with the children, the first microphone was already live.

qa.q: Where did Payal keep the backup steps for patching the choir?
qa.a: On a laminated card taped inside the second drawer.

qa.q: How can you tell Payal was scared at first, and what calmed her?
qa.a: Her chest tightened and she stared at the desk, feeling panicky; the memory of her card steadied her, and she felt calmer once she saw forgetting a March setup as normal.

qa.q: What small habit helped Payal most, and how could she make it stronger?
qa.a: Rewriting the card every few weeks kept it ready; she could also keep a paper copy near the generator in case both power and phone fail.

qa.q: What would change for Reena and the children if Payal had blamed herself instead?
qa.a: Payal might have frozen or rushed, and Reena would have walked in to a studio that was not ready, with nervous children waiting.

grounding: Illustrates a working adult relying on a regularly refreshed note under time pressure and accepting that an unused skill had faded.

passage: Vikas found Maria at her desk in the Pune office with her head in her hands. "I've forgotten how to join two tables," she said. "I did it in college every week. I'm useless." Vikas pulled up a chair and opened a file on his laptop called Things I Keep Losing. It had forty short entries, each with a date. "I read five of these every Friday with my chai," he said. "Look, I've re-learnt joins three times this year." Maria laughed a little. "You're not embarrassed?" "Why would I be? My head throws out what I'm not using. That's its job. I just make it easy to find again." He showed her how he tagged each entry by how often he needed it. By lunch Maria had started her own file, with one line in it.

qa.q: What was the name of the file Vikas opened on his laptop?
qa.a: The file was called Things I Keep Losing.

qa.q: Why does Vikas feel calm rather than embarrassed about re-learning joins?
qa.a: He feels relaxed and secure because he sees his mind throwing out unused things as its normal job, and his Friday review makes the skills easy to find again.

qa.q: What could Maria try this week to stop feeling useless about forgotten skills?
qa.a: She could add a short entry each time she re-learns something and read a few of them at a set time each week, as Vikas does.

qa.q: How does Maria see her forgetting before Vikas shows her the file?
qa.a: Maria sees it as proof that she is useless, because she expected a college skill to stay forever without practice.

grounding: Shows a young professional keeping dated notes, reviewing them weekly, and treating forgetting as the mind's normal clearing-out.

passage: It rained all morning, so recess at Keerthana's new school in Bengaluru happened inside, in a hot, noisy classroom. Keerthana sat by the window while the others played a clapping game she did not know. When Reena came over, Keerthana said, "In my old school in Coimbatore, nobody ever fought. We all shared everything." Reena nodded. "Even the swing?" Keerthana opened her mouth, then shut it. There had been a swing, and there had been Abinaya, who never let anyone else on it, and that one day Keerthana cried behind the water tank. "Well," she said slowly, "mostly." She still missed the old classroom with the fan that squeaked. But she let Reena teach her the first clap.

qa.q: Why did recess happen inside the classroom?
qa.a: Because it rained all morning.

qa.q: Why does Keerthana feel lonely and remember her old school as perfect?
qa.a: She feels left out while the others play a game she does not know, so the old school, where she belonged, seems warm and free of fights.

qa.q: What could help Keerthana settle into the new class?
qa.a: She could keep saying yes to small invitations like Reena's clapping game, and remember that her old class also had hard days.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Keerthana says nobody ever fought at the old school?
qa.a: Reena might feel a little doubtful, and maybe worried that the new class seems worse to Keerthana, which could be why she comes over to include her.

grounding: Shows a child who has moved schools picturing the old class as perfect until a question brings back a forgotten quarrel.

passage: Darshan pushed his dal around the plate in their new flat in Thane. "At my Nashik school everyone was my friend," he told his big sister, Sarita. "Here nobody even says hi." Sarita raised an eyebrow. "Everyone? What about Ronak, who ate your tiffin every single day?" "That was only once." "You came home crying about it every week, Darshan. Aai had to write a note to the teacher." Darshan frowned. He could see the old classroom clearly: the mango tree outside, his seat by the door, the drawing of the tiger he made. Ronak was blurry, like a smudge on a photograph. "Maybe twice," he said. Sarita smiled and passed him the papad. "You'll have new tigers to draw here too." Darshan did not answer, but he ate the papad.

qa.q: Who used to eat Darshan's tiffin at the Nashik school?
qa.a: Ronak ate Darshan's tiffin.

qa.q: Why does Darshan honestly think the tiffin trouble happened only once?
qa.a: He misses his old school and feels sad in the new flat, so the happy parts like the mango tree and the tiger drawing feel clear while the upsetting parts have gone blurry.

qa.q: How could Sarita help Darshan without making him feel silly?
qa.a: She could agree that he misses the old school and then ask what he would like to find at the new one, like a place to draw 🙂

qa.q: How does Sarita see Darshan's picture of the old school?
qa.a: Sarita remembers the weekly crying and Aai's note, so she sees that his memory has smoothed the hard parts away and gently wants him to see the whole picture.

grounding: Shows a child in a new city remembering the old class as all friendship while forgetting the repeated tiffin trouble.

passage:
"Vijay bhaiya, my old school had the best library in the world."
"The one with six shelves?"
"It had the best books. And Mrs Dsouza read to us every Friday."
"You told me she shouted when you dropped the atlas."
"She didn't shout. She just said it loudly."
Vijay laughed. "Nandini, you hated that library for a whole month."
"No I didn't."
"You said the dust made you sneeze and the big boys hid the comics."
Nandini hugged her knees on the sofa. "It was still better than here. Here I don't know where anything is."
"Ah." Vijay sat down beside her. "So the new library is hard because it's new."
"Maybe."
"Want to go on Saturday and find the comics together?"
Nandini shrugged, but she was already thinking about which shelf they would be on.

qa.q: Who read to the class every Friday at Nandini's old school?
qa.a: Mrs Dsouza read to them every Friday.

qa.q: What does Nandini's hugging her knees suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels lost and a bit lonely in the new library, so the old one seems perfect because she knew where everything was there.

qa.q: Which part of Vijay's approach works, and why?
qa.a: Offering to visit the new library with her on Saturday works better than only correcting her memory, because it tackles the real problem of feeling lost.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Nandini's memory of the old library?
qa.a: Vijay sees that she is leaving out the dust, the hidden comics and the loud teacher, but he also understands she is uneasy about the new school.

grounding: Shows a child calling the old school library the best while forgetting the troubles she once complained about.

passage: The power cut came at nine, two days before Bhavna's physics board exam. She lit a candle, stared at the formula sheet, and gave up. Ishita, revising in the same room for the same paper, heard her sigh. "I just want to be five again," Bhavna said. "No exams, no marks, just the swing in Nani's courtyard and mangoes." Ishita put down her pen. "You? At five? You screamed every time the lights went off. Your mum had to sleep with you." Bhavna laughed, then went quiet. She did remember that, a little: the dark stairwell, the thunder, being too small to reach the switch. "I guess I just remember the mangoes," she said. The candle flickered. She picked the sheet back up, holding it closer to the flame.

qa.q: When did the power cut happen?
qa.a: At nine, two days before Bhavna's physics board exam.

qa.q: Why does being five again feel so appealing to Bhavna?
qa.a: She feels pressured and tired before the board exam, so early childhood seems carefree, with only the swing and mangoes, and her old fears have faded from view.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do the next time the longing for childhood hits during revision?
qa.a: She could name what is heavy right now, take a short break, and plan one small task instead of comparing the present to a smoothed-over past.

qa.q: How does Ishita see Bhavna's wish to be five?
qa.a: Ishita remembers Bhavna screaming in the dark, so she sees the wish as leaving out the fears, and she gently reminds her with a joke.

grounding: Shows a teenager under exam pressure longing for a carefree childhood while forgetting how frightened she was then.

passage: Nazia found the old photo album while clearing the loft of their Hyderabad flat, the week her coaching schedule doubled. There she was at six in a frilly frock, grinning on a giant wheel. She sat on the dusty floor for twenty minutes. "Life was so easy then," she told her brother Farhan when he climbed up to help. "No tests, no ranks, nobody expecting anything." Farhan peered at the photo. "You cried because you were too short for that ride. Abba had to take the photo while it was standing still." Nazia snorted. "Rubbish." "And you were terrified of the school van driver's moustache." She looked again. Her grin did look a little stiff. Still, she slid the photo into her pencil box before going back to her maths notes.

qa.q: What did Nazia find while clearing the loft?
qa.a: She found the old photo album.

qa.q: Why did Nazia sit on the floor with the album for twenty minutes?
qa.a: She felt worn down by the doubled coaching schedule, and the photo made childhood look easy, so she felt a warm longing for a time when nobody expected anything of her.

qa.q: What small step could help Nazia with the coaching pressure itself?
qa.a: She could tell a parent or teacher how heavy the new schedule feels and ask for help planning breaks, rather than only escaping into old photos.

qa.q: How does Farhan see the photo differently from Nazia?
qa.a: Farhan remembers the tears about being too short and the fear of the van driver, so he sees the grin as less carefree than Nazia remembers.

grounding: Shows a teenager under study pressure longing for a childhood she remembers as easy while forgetting its fears and limits.

passage:
"Didi, remember when all I had to do was colour and nap?"
Alka looked up from her laptop. "Tanvir, you're seventeen. Nobody's making you nap."
"I'm serious. Class seven onwards it's just tests. When I was small nobody cared about my marks."
"You cared. You cried because Pinky got a gold star and you didn't."
"That's different."
"And you wouldn't sleep without the corridor light on until you were nine."
Tanvir groaned into a cushion. "Why do you remember everything?"
"Because I was the one who had to leave it on." She closed the laptop. "What's actually going on?"
"The mock results come out tomorrow."
"Okay. So being little looks good because tomorrow looks scary."
Tanvir didn't answer, but he stopped hiding his face.

qa.q: When do Tanvir's mock results come out?
qa.a: The mock results come out tomorrow.

qa.q: What is Tanvir worried about underneath his wish to be small again?
qa.a: He feels anxious about tomorrow's mock results, and that fear makes early childhood seem free of pressure.

qa.q: What did Alka do that helped Tanvir, and what could she add?
qa.a: She asked what was actually going on, which uncovered his worry; she could now help him plan how he will handle the results, whatever they are.

qa.q: If you were Alka, how would it feel to hear Tanvir call childhood easy?
qa.a: It might feel a bit funny and tender, since Alka remembers leaving the corridor light on for him and knows he had real fears back then too.

grounding: Shows a teenager longing for early childhood before a stressful result while forgetting the fears and jealousies of that time.

passage:
Week one. Naveen called home from the hostel in Kanpur every night. He told Amma the mess dal was water and his old gang in Nagpur were the only real friends he'd ever have. When Anjali, from his lab section, invited him to the robotics club sign-up, he said he was busy and scrolled through old photos instead.
Week three. His lab group had to present on Friday. Naveen skipped the Wednesday meeting to watch videos of Nagpur rain. Anjali texted, "We need your slide."
Week six. On a call, his brother mentioned that the old gang had stopped replying to each other months ago. Naveen went quiet. He remembered the fights over the one scooter too. The next morning he knocked on Anjali's door and asked when the robotics club met. He still missed Amma's dal.

qa.q: Where was Naveen's old gang?
qa.a: His old gang was in Nagpur.

qa.q: Why did scrolling old photos feel better to Naveen than going to the club sign-up?
qa.a: He felt homesick and unsure in the new hostel, so the warm, idealised picture of home felt safer than facing strangers and new tasks.

qa.q: What could Naveen do on the nights he misses home most?
qa.a: He could keep calling home and still attend one club meeting or group session that week, so missing home does not stop him from building a life at the hostel.

qa.q: How might Anjali have seen Naveen during the first weeks?
qa.a: Anjali might have felt frustrated when he skipped the meeting, and puzzled by someone who kept saying he was busy while the group waited on his slide.

grounding: Shows a hostel student idealising home and old friends while avoiding present tasks, and slowly seeing a more mixed picture.

passage: Pema, come, sit with your Madhav chacha. You say the hostel food is terrible and everyone back home is wonderful. I said the same, in 1989, at the college in Pune. I was eighteen. Every Friday I took the night bus back to our village, and every Monday I came back tired. My friends at home, I thought, were brothers, and my hostel roommate Deepak was just a stranger who snored. The debate team trials came and went. I didn't even try. Then one Friday the bus broke down and I stayed. Deepak took me to the canteen, and we argued about cricket till two in the morning. I realised the village friends had also argued with me, and teased me, and forgot my birthday. That Sunday I signed up for debates. I still missed home. I just stopped hiding in it.

qa.q: Where did Madhav go to college?
qa.a: Madhav went to the college in Pune.

qa.q: Why did the weekly bus home feel so important to young Madhav?
qa.a: Young Madhav felt homesick and lonely, and going home was a way to avoid a new place where the roommate felt like a stranger and the debate trials felt risky.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The night the bus broke down forced Madhav to stay, and the long talk with Deepak showed him the hostel could hold real friendship too.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt about Madhav leaving every Friday?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt shut out or unsure whether Madhav liked him, since his roommate kept disappearing and called only the village friends real.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a hostel student idealising home and old friends while quietly avoiding challenges at college.

passage: Diwali week, and Nandini was stuck in the Delhi hostel. The floods had cancelled her train to Lucknow, and the end-semester exams started on Monday anyway. She sat on her bed looking at the family group chat: rangoli photos, Mamma's gulab jamun, her school friends at the old chai stall. "Everything good is there," she told Sachin in the empty reading room. "Here I'm just a roll number." Sachin, also stuck, raised an eyebrow. "Didn't you tell me your school friends never visited when you had dengue?" Nandini picked at a thread on her dupatta. "That was one time." "And you left Lucknow because you wanted this course." She was quiet. Then she opened her notes. "Fine. Revise with me, and we'll make terrible tea at nine." It wasn't home. It was something.

qa.q: Why couldn't Nandini travel to Lucknow for Diwali?
qa.a: The floods had cancelled her train, and her exams started on Monday.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling as she looked at the family group chat?
qa.a: She felt homesick and a bit resentful of the hostel, longing for home, so everything there looked good and her present life looked empty.

qa.q: What could Nandini try for the rest of the stuck week?
qa.a: She could plan small shared things with people who are also in the hostel, like revising and tea with Sachin, while still calling home.

qa.q: What would change if Sachin had only agreed that everything good is at home?
qa.a: Nandini would probably sink further into missing home and avoid her revision, instead of turning back to her notes and the people around her.

grounding: Shows a hostel student, kept from home by floods and exams, idealising home and old friends while stepping back from present work.

passage: At the Friday gathering in the senior citizens' day centre, Rafiq was setting out chairs when Gurpreet Aunty began. "In our time, nobody locked their doors. Everyone helped everyone. Children respected elders." Two others nodded. Rafiq, who ran the centre's activities, remembered her story from last month: walking four kilometres for water, the year the canal flooded, how her brother had to leave school to work. He almost said so. Instead he sat down. "Who helped you most back then, Aunty?" Her face softened. She talked about a neighbour who shared her last sack of wheat. Rafiq listened, asking one more question, then another. The past she described was easier than the one she had told him before. But the kindness in it was real, and the whole table was smiling.

qa.q: How far did Gurpreet Aunty once say she walked for water?
qa.a: Four kilometres.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq feel tempted to correct Gurpreet Aunty, and why did he hold back?
qa.a: He felt uneasy because he remembered her harder stories, but he cared more about her warm memory and the mood at the table than about winning the point.

qa.q: What makes Rafiq's question a good choice?
qa.a: Asking who helped her most invites the real kindness in her memory without arguing about whether the old days were easier 🤍

qa.q: How might Gurpreet Aunty feel when Rafiq asks about the people who helped her?
qa.a: She likely feels respected and warm, since someone younger wants to hear her memory instead of doubting it.

grounding: Shows a young professional hearing an elder praise the old days, noticing the hardship left out, and choosing to listen kindly.

passage:
Subject: Nana's stories, again

Hi Dhruv,

Remember how you groaned at Eid lunch when Nana started on "In our days, a rupee bought a feast and nobody was ever lonely"? I groaned too, inside. You know the family story, how he left school at twelve to mind the shop, and how the whole street went hungry the drought year.

But I was watching his face while he talked, and he was glowing. He wasn't lying. He was remembering being young, his friends on the rooftop, Nani laughing.

So I've decided something. When he does it next time, I'm not going to say "But Nana, what about the drought?" I'm going to ask what they played on the roof. We can have the history argument with a textbook. We only get so many lunches with him.

See you at Diwali,
Nazia

qa.q: At what age did Nana leave school to mind the shop?
qa.a: He left school at twelve.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling while watching Nana's face at lunch?
qa.a: Nazia felt a mix of irritation and tenderness: annoyed by the rosy story at first, then moved by how Nana glowed while remembering being young.

qa.q: What plan does Nazia make for the next lunch, and why might it work?
qa.a: Nazia plans to ask what they played on the roof instead of correcting him, which honours the warm memory and keeps the lunch friendly.

qa.q: How might Nana feel if the grandchildren kept correcting his stories with the drought?
qa.a: He might feel dismissed or hurt, as if his happy memories of youth and friends did not count.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing an elder's golden picture of the past, accepting the warmth as real, and choosing kind listening over argument.

passage: Yash, you asked Indu from the accounts team what surprised me most in my first office job. Honestly? The lunch table. I'm the youngest in our accounts team in Kochi, and every day Joseph sir says, "In my time, we did everything by hand and never made mistakes. Young people today depend on machines." The first week I wanted to jump in. I'd seen the old ledgers in the storeroom. They're full of crossings-out. Red ink everywhere. But then I noticed how Joseph sir's voice changes when he talks about that office, the typewriter noise, his old boss who gave him a chance. It's not about accuracy. It's about who he was then. So now I just ask about the old boss. And last week, he asked me to show him the new spreadsheet. He'd never asked before.

qa.q: What did the narrator find in the old ledgers in the storeroom?
qa.a: They're full of crossings-out, with red ink everywhere.

qa.q: Why did Indu want to jump in during the first week, and what changed that feeling?
qa.a: Indu felt irritated, knowing the ledgers had mistakes, but then felt touched noticing Joseph sir's voice change as he spoke about his old boss and who he was then.

qa.q: Which approach worked better with Joseph sir, and why?
qa.a: Asking about his old boss instead of arguing about accuracy worked, because it valued his memory and built the trust that led him to ask about the spreadsheet.

qa.q: How might Joseph sir feel when the youngest colleague listens instead of correcting him?
qa.a: He may feel respected and less threatened by the new ways, which could be why he finally asked to see the spreadsheet.

grounding: Shows a young professional hearing a senior colleague praise the old days, seeing the warmth is real though the past was messier, and listening kindly.

passage: Sarika walked with her cousin Baljeet along the canal road outside their village near Moga, past the old peepal where they used to hide in summer. "Remember the mangoes from Tayaji's orchard? The whole gang, barefoot?" Baljeet grinned. "And now children just sit on phones." Sarika laughed, then stopped herself. She remembered the other things too: the walk to the one-room school through ankle-deep mud, the roof that leaked on their slates, the winter her friend Gurmeet left school for good. "The mangoes were the best part," she said. "The mud was not." Now she taught in the new school at the crossing, and the children came on a bus. She still kept one thing from those summers: on the last day of term she took her class to the orchard, barefoot if they liked.

qa.q: Where did Sarika now teach?
qa.a: In the new school at the crossing.

qa.q: Why does Sarika stop herself after laughing at Baljeet's comment?
qa.a: She feels fond of the memories but also uneasy with the complaint, because she remembers the mud, the leaking roof and her friend leaving school, and does not want the past to make today look poor.

qa.q: How does Sarika keep the good of the old summers without letting them shrink the present?
qa.a: She enjoys the memory and keeps a value from it, the orchard trip, while remembering the hardships, so she can appreciate the new school and bus too.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see the children of today compared with Sarika?
qa.a: Baljeet seems to see them as missing out, stuck on phones, because the mango summers are remembered without the mud and the leaking roof.

grounding: Shows a young adult enjoying village nostalgia as comfort and a source of values while recalling what was hard, so the present does not seem poor.

passage: Sunday afternoon in Durban, and Dalia had the old playlist from her student days on while she cooked. "This song," she told her flatmate Zanele, swaying. "Third year, the flat on Umbilo Road. We'd make a giant pot of soup and whoever was broke that week ate free." Zanele smiled. "Sounds like heaven." Dalia stirred and thought about it. The flat had also had a broken geyser for five months. She'd cried in the bathroom before every exam. She had once been so lonely she spoke to nobody for a whole weekend. "It was heaven sometimes," she said. "Mostly it was the soup." She looked at the pot. "Actually, why don't we do that here? Sunday soup, anyone from the building can come." Zanele was already writing the note for the lift.

qa.q: What did Dalia and her friends cook in the Umbilo Road flat?
qa.a: They made a giant pot of soup.

qa.q: What is Dalia feeling as she stirs the pot and remembers the old flat?
qa.a: She feels warm and nostalgic about the soup nights but also a little sad, remembering the broken geyser, the exam tears and the lonely weekend.

qa.q: Which choice turns Dalia's nostalgia into something useful?
qa.a: She keeps the value from the past, sharing soup with whoever needs it, and brings it into her present life instead of just mourning the old flat.

qa.q: How might Zanele experience the new Sunday soup plan?
qa.a: Zanele seems excited and included, since Dalia's memory turns into something they can share now rather than a story she can only listen to.

grounding: Shows a young adult enjoying nostalgia for student life while honestly recalling its hardships and carrying its best value into the present.

passage: In the staff room of the Jaipur school, the talk turned to college. Vinita, who taught maths, sighed. "Those were the golden years. No parents' meetings, no marking." Kiran, twenty-six and three years into teaching English, felt the pull too: hostel terrace, late-night songs, everyone sharing tiffins. She let herself enjoy it for a moment. Then she remembered the rest: the night before finals when she couldn't breathe for worry, the roommate who stopped speaking to her, her father's illness in second year. "Golden, and also terrifying," she said. Vinita laughed. "True. I failed stats once." Kiran opened her tiffin and pushed it into the middle of the table. "The sharing part we can still do." Vinita added her aloo parathas. The bell rang, and neither of them rushed.

qa.q: What subject did Vinita teach?
qa.a: Vinita taught maths.

qa.q: Why did Kiran let herself enjoy the college memory before remembering the hard parts?
qa.a: She felt warm and comforted by the hostel memories, and enjoying them felt safe because she also knew to recall the worry, the roommate and her father's illness.

qa.q: What small step did Kiran take to carry the best of the past into the present?
qa.a: She pushed her tiffin into the middle of the table so the staff could share, keeping the value of college days without mourning them.

qa.q: How does Vinita's view of college change during the conversation?
qa.a: Vinita starts by calling college the golden years, but after Kiran's honest reply she admits failing stats and joins in sharing food.

grounding: Shows a young teacher enjoying nostalgia while reminding herself of past hardship so that her present working life does not seem poor.

passage: After cricket practice at the Lucknow sports club, Coach Pankaj found Mohit sitting alone on the pavilion steps. Mohit had been bowled out first ball. "How's your week been?" Coach asked. "Bad," Mohit said. "I got a sum wrong on Monday. My bat handle broke. Today I got out. And tomorrow's match will be bad too." Coach sat down. "What about Tuesday's catch? The whole team cheered." Mohit blinked. He had forgotten the catch completely. "And didn't your Nani visit?" "Yes," Mohit said slowly. "She brought laddoos." He still felt sad about getting out. But the week had some good bits hiding in it. Coach handed him a ball. "Ten throws before your papa comes?" Mohit stood up, wiping his nose on his sleeve.

qa.q: What happened to Mohit's bat on his bad week?
qa.a: His bat handle broke.

qa.q: Why did Mohit only remember bad things when Coach asked about his week?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed after being bowled out first ball, and that sadness made the bad moments come to mind first, hiding the catch and his Nani's visit.

qa.q: How could Coach Pankaj help Mohit next time he is upset?
qa.a: He could ask Mohit to name one good thing from the week alongside the hard ones, as he did with the catch and the laddoos.

qa.q: How might Mohit's teammates remember Tuesday differently?
qa.a: They might remember Tuesday as a happy day, since the whole team cheered Mohit's catch.

grounding: Shows a child whose sad mood after a bad game lets only the bad moments of the week come to mind and makes tomorrow seem sure to go badly.

passage:
Monday: Jagdish's new kite tore on the neem tree before it even flew. He sat on the roof and would not come down for dinner.
Tuesday: At school, Yash asked, "How was your weekend?" "Horrible," Jagdish said. "Everything went wrong. And the kite competition on Sunday will be horrible too." Yash looked confused. "But you won at carrom on Saturday. You beat my brother." Jagdish shrugged. It did not feel like it had happened.
Friday: His uncle helped him glue the torn paper, and the kite flew over three rooftops. That evening Jagdish told his mother about the weekend: the carrom win, the jalebis at the fair, Yash's cousin's funny dog. "Wasn't it a horrible weekend?" she teased. Jagdish frowned. "Was it?" Then he laughed and ran back up to the roof.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish's new kite tear?
qa.a: It tore on the neem tree.

qa.q: Why did the carrom win not feel real to Jagdish on Tuesday?
qa.a: He was still upset about his torn kite, and his sad mood only let the bad moments feel real, so the happy win seemed far away.

qa.q: What could Yash do when a friend says everything went wrong?
qa.a: He could gently remind them of one good thing that happened, as he did with the carrom win, and maybe offer to help with the problem.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's mother see his weekend on Friday compared with Tuesday?
qa.a: She hears about the carrom, the jalebis and the funny dog, so she sees a happy weekend and is amused that he once called it horrible.

grounding: Shows a child's sad mood choosing only bad memories and a gloomy forecast, and a better mood later bringing the good memories back.

passage: Lalremsiami, you are sulking about your week? Come, let your Hafsa aunty tell you something. When I was nine, in Aizawl, I cracked my slate on Tuesday and my teacher scolded me in front of everyone. I cried the whole way home. That night I told my father, "This whole week was bad. On Monday I lost my ribbon, on Wednesday it rained, and the fair on Saturday will be bad also." My father did not argue. He asked me, "What did you eat on Thursday?" I said, "Egg curry," and I remembered: my friend Mawii had shared her egg because it was my favourite. Then I remembered I sang in assembly. By the end I was laughing. And the fair was lovely. The week had not changed. Only my sad eyes had.

qa.q: What did young Hafsa crack on Tuesday?
qa.a: She cracked her slate.

qa.q: Why did the whole week seem bad to young Hafsa that night?
qa.a: She was hurt and ashamed after being scolded in front of everyone, so her sadness picked out only the bad moments and made the fair seem sure to be bad too.

qa.q: What choice did Hafsa's father make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He did not argue but asked what she ate on Thursday, which gently led her to remember Mawii's kindness and the singing on her own.

qa.q: How might Mawii have felt about the week if asked?
qa.a: Mawii might remember a happy moment of sharing her egg with a friend, since the egg curry was a kind thing she chose to do.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's childhood memory, how a sad mood made a child recall only bad things and expect the fair to be bad too.

passage: So, Kalyani, you want Tanvir's honest version of class eleven. For about two months I was low, like a grey filter on everything. A friend would text "ok" and I'd read it as "go away." Someone didn't save me a seat, and I decided the whole class was done with me. If you'd asked about my year, I'd have listed every test I bombed and not one good thing. And it felt like fact. That's the scary part. It didn't feel like a mood, it felt like seeing clearly. My Ammi noticed I'd stopped eating with the family. One evening she sat on my bed and asked straight out how long I'd been feeling like this. The next day we went to the school counsellor together, and then to a doctor. Slowly, "ok" went back to meaning ok.

qa.q: How long did Tanvir say the low period in class eleven lasted?
qa.a: For about two months.

qa.q: Why did reading "ok" as "go away" feel so true to Tanvir at the time?
qa.a: The low mood made everything look rejecting and hopeless, and Tanvir felt sad and alone, so the gloomy reading felt like seeing clearly rather than like a feeling.

qa.q: What did Ammi do well, and what could a friend do in a similar situation?
qa.a: Ammi asked directly how long it had been going on and took the next step to the counsellor and a doctor; a friend could tell a trusted adult rather than keep quiet.

qa.q: How might the friend who texted "ok" have seen that message?
qa.a: The friend probably meant nothing more than ok, and may have felt confused or hurt if Tanvir pulled away because of it.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose low mood turned neutral messages into rejection and only failures into memory, and an adult who got caring professional help.

passage:
Monday. Sudha texted Rekha before school: "Can't walk with you today." Rekha stared at the screen. She's tired of me, she thought, like everyone. On the bus she replayed every bad mark she'd got that term and couldn't think of one good one.
Thursday. Rekha had eaten lunch alone for four days, head on the desk. Her class teacher, Mrs Pillai, kept her back after the bell. "You've seemed very down for a while, Rekha. I'm worried about you." Rekha's eyes filled. That afternoon Mrs Pillai called Rekha's parents and walked her to the school counsellor, who met all three of them before the day ended.
Two weeks later. After a few talks with the counsellor, Rekha scrolled back to Monday's message. Underneath it was a second one she'd skipped: "Dentist, ugh. Save me a seat at lunch?" She still had grey days. But she could see this one differently now.

qa.q: What did Sudha's Monday text say?
qa.a: "Can't walk with you today."

qa.q: Why did Rekha believe Sudha was tired of her?
qa.a: Rekha was in a low, lonely mood, so the plain message felt like rejection and only her failures came to mind, making the gloomy reading feel like fact.

qa.q: Which of Mrs Pillai's steps mattered most, and why?
qa.a: She named her worry kindly, called Rekha's parents the same day and took her to the counsellor, instead of waiting to see if it passed.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel if she learned Rekha had read her text as rejection?
qa.a: Sudha would likely feel surprised and sorry, since she only had a dentist visit and was even asking Rekha to save her a seat.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a low mood reading a neutral message as rejection and recalling only failures, and adults giving caring professional help.

passage: Jeevan, you think nobody understands being sixteen and miserable? Your Damini atya does. When I was fifteen, in Kolhapur, I went through a long grey time. My best friend didn't wave to me across the market once, and I decided she hated me. I wrote a list in my notebook of every mistake I'd made since class five. Every page felt like proof. My aunt, the one who lived with us, noticed I'd stopped singing while I cleaned rice. She didn't say "cheer up." She asked how many weeks it had been, and I said I didn't know, many. The very next morning she took me to our family doctor, who sent me to speak with someone trained in this. It took months. My friend, it turned out, had forgotten her glasses that day.

qa.q: Why hadn't Damini's friend waved to her in the market?
qa.a: Her friend had forgotten her glasses that day.

qa.q: Why did the list of mistakes feel like proof to young Damini?
qa.a: She was in a long low mood, sad and hopeless, which made her recall only failures and made those gloomy judgments feel like facts.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why was it a wise choice?
qa.a: Her aunt asked how long it had been and took her to the doctor the next morning, which brought in trained help instead of just telling her to cheer up.

qa.q: How might the aunt have felt noticing Damini had stopped singing?
qa.a: The aunt likely felt worried and caring, since a small change in a daily habit told her something was wrong.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager's low mood turning a neutral moment into rejection, and an adult seeking professional help.

passage:
Diary, 11 p.m.

I GOT THE INTERNSHIP. Madhuri from Room 14, summer analyst, actual stipend. I screamed in the corridor.

Then, in one afternoon, I said yes to:
- running the cultural fest decoration team (they asked, I was glowing, why not?)
- tutoring Bhupen's cousin for board maths, three evenings a week
- the Himachal trek in May, even though the internship starts in May
- rewriting the club newsletter by Sunday

It all felt easy. Like I had extra hours hidden somewhere. Bhupen asked, "Are you sure about the trek dates?" and I laughed and said I'd manage.

Now I'm looking at the calendar and May has two of me in it. Also mid-sems are next week, which I forgot existed.

Tomorrow, when I'm less buzzy, I'll go through this list again. Some of these yeses need to become "actually, sorry."

qa.q: What was the first thing Madhuri said yes to after the internship news?
qa.a: Running the cultural fest decoration team.

qa.q: Why did all those yeses feel easy to Madhuri at the time?
qa.a: Madhuri was thrilled and glowing about the internship, and that happy mood made every task seem light and every clash look manageable.

qa.q: What could Madhuri do tomorrow to fix the overload?
qa.a: Madhuri could check each yes against the calendar and the mid-sems, keep the ones that fit, and politely withdraw from the clashing ones soon.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Madhuri's quick yes to the trek?
qa.a: Bhupen seems doubtful and a little concerned, since Bhupen noticed the date clash and got only a laugh in return.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a joyful mood underestimating risks and clashes and agreeing to far too many commitments.

passage: The results came the morning of the village fair near Thanjavur: Kavitha had topped her college. By noon she was floating. She told her aunt Usha she would cook for the whole family's pooja tomorrow, all forty people. She promised the headmaster she'd teach the evening class for the fair week. When her cousins said the last bus back to college left at ten tonight and was often empty, she said, "I'll take it, no problem, I'm not scared of anything today." Usha watched her over the sweet stall. "Kavitha, your practical is tomorrow morning. And the pooja is also tomorrow." Kavitha laughed, then stopped. "Oh." Usha squeezed her arm. "Be happy. Then decide with a cup of tea." Kavitha asked her uncle to ride with her to the bus stand, and gave the pooja to her cousins.

qa.q: What did Kavitha promise the headmaster?
qa.a: She promised to teach the evening class for the fair week.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha feel she could do everything that day?
qa.a: She was delighted and proud after topping her college, and the joy made risks like the late empty bus and the clashing dates seem tiny.

qa.q: What small step did Usha suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Usha suggested deciding over a cup of tea, which gives the happy mood time to settle so Kavitha can check dates and risks clearly.

qa.q: How might Usha see Kavitha's promises at the fair?
qa.a: Usha seems fond and proud but also concerned, noticing the clashes and the late bus that Kavitha's high spirits were hiding.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose great mood makes risks look small and leads her to promise too much until an elder helps her pause.

passage: I'm Chandrika, and last March I typed my resignation in eleven minutes. Bhupen, my manager, had cut me off in the client meeting and taken credit for the design I'd spent three weeks on. I was shaking with anger at my desk. The email was ready, cursor on Send. Then I saw my reflection in the dark monitor, jaw tight, face red, and I thought: this isn't a decision, this is a temperature. I saved the draft and walked round the block twice. I didn't answer Bhupen's "all good?" message either. Next morning, calm, I read the draft again. Half of it was true. Half was just heat. Instead of resigning, I asked Bhupen for twenty minutes and told him, plainly, that I needed my name on my work. He agreed. I still have the draft. It reminds me to wait.

qa.q: How long did the narrator spend on the design Bhupen took credit for?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she saw her reflection in the monitor?
qa.a: Chandrika was still furious, but seeing the tight jaw and red face made her wary of acting in that heat, so she felt the need to pause.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saving the draft and rereading it the next morning worked, because calm let Chandrika separate the true complaint from the anger and ask Bhupen directly for credit.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen things if the resignation had been sent that afternoon?
qa.a: Bhupen might have been shocked and defensive, never learning the real issue about credit, and the chance to fix it would have been lost.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing anger, postponing a resignation and a message, and returning calm to find the view had changed.

passage:
Coach's note, Saturday, city athletics club.
Vinita finished last in the 800 m today after leading at the bell. She came off the track, red-faced, and told me she was quitting the club. Then she pulled out her phone and started typing to Noor, her relay partner, who had skipped the warm-up with her. I could see the message was long. I didn't take the phone. I said, "Big decisions after a race tend to be about the race." She looked at me hard. Then she put the phone in her bag, walked a slow lap alone and stretched. Before leaving she said, "I'll decide on Monday." On Monday she came to practice early. She said she had deleted the message and asked Noor to warm up with her instead. Noor said yes. I've kept her on the relay list.

qa.q: When did Vinita come back to practice after the race?
qa.a: On Monday, early.

qa.q: What does Vinita putting the phone in her bag suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: Though she was still angry and upset, it suggests she recognised she was not calm enough to decide or send the long message just then.

qa.q: How could a coach support an athlete who wants to quit right after a bad race?
qa.a: The coach can stay calm, avoid taking over, and point out that choices made in the heat of a race often change, as this note shows.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt if the long message had been sent that afternoon?
qa.a: Noor might have felt hurt or blamed, and the relay partnership could have cracked over something Vinita later chose to let go.

grounding: Shows, through an observer's note, a young adult pausing a major choice and an angry message until she is calm, and seeing her view change.

passage:
Dear diary, Ankita here, and it's a bad night.

The fellowship rejected my proposal. Two years of work, a three-line email. I sat on the terrace and decided I'm done with research. I'll withdraw from the programme, tell Shankar I'm not applying anywhere again, and join Papa's office like everyone always said I would.

I've got the withdrawal form open in another tab right now.

But I also know this feeling. Last year after the conference rejection I nearly deleted my whole thesis folder, and a week later I was glad I hadn't.

So here's the deal. I'm writing this down instead of filling the form. No texts to Shankar tonight either; he'd only worry. I'll read this again on Sunday after sleeping properly and walking to the lake.

If I still want to quit then, I'll talk it through with my guide first.

qa.q: How long had Ankita worked on the rejected proposal?
qa.a: Two years of work.

qa.q: Why does Ankita choose to write in the diary instead of filling in the form?
qa.a: Ankita feels hopeless and crushed tonight but also recognises this despair from last year, and wants to wait until calmer before acting.

qa.q: What makes Ankita's plan for Sunday a sensible one?
qa.a: Ankita sets a clear time to revisit the choice after sleep and a walk, and plans to talk to the guide before any final step.

qa.q: What would change for Shankar if Ankita texted him tonight?
qa.a: Shankar would likely feel worried and caught off guard by a sudden message about quitting, written in the worst hour of Ankita's disappointment.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing despair, postponing a major choice and messages, and planning to return when calm to see if the view has changed.
